Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Identify the clinical manifestations of cervical radiculopathy.
Assess the natural history of cervical radiculopathy.
Define the differential diagnosis for patients in whom cervical radiculopathy is suspected.
Implement surgical and nonsurgical management for cervical radiculopathy.
Cervical Radiculopathy
Overview
Definition: constellation of symptoms, including pain, numbness, and/or weakness that result
from compression and inflammation of a nerve root in the cervical spine. Classically includes
radiating symptoms in the corresponding dermatome, with or without associated neck pain.

Epidemiology
Incidence ranges from 63.5 to 179 per 100,000 person-years.
As many as 26% of patients with symptoms of radiculopathy ultimately require surgical
treatment.
Peak age is 50 to 54 years.
History of trauma or physical exertion immediately leading to symptoms in 15% of patients

Epidemiology
Cervical radiculopathy is one of the most common spine conditions in the United States.
Depending on the cited study, the incidence of cervical radiculopathy ranges from 63.5
to 179 per 100,000 person-years. The condition is most prevalent in patients aged 50 to
54 years and typically is related to degenerative changes within the cervical spine. A
history of trauma or a specific event leading to radicular symptoms is present in only
15% of patients.
Anatomy
Ventral and dorsal roots arise from the spinal cord and join to form a cervical spinal nerve.
Each cervical spinal nerve exits the foramen above the same numbered pedicle, except the C8
nerve root, which exits above the first thoracic pedicle. The exiting root traverses the foramen
in a ventrolateral direction.
Borders of the cervical neuroforamen include the uncovertebral joint (ventromedial), vertebral
artery (lateral), inferior and superior articular processes of vertebra above and below
(dorsolateral), and suprajacent pedicle (superior) (Figure 1).

Cervical radiculopathy results from compression of the nerve roots or the spinal nerve
as they exit the neuroforamen. The ventral and dorsal nerve roots arise from the spinal
cord and join to form a cervical spinal nerve. Each nerve exits above the same numbered
pedicle in the cervical spine. For example, the C6 nerve exits above the C6 pedicle at the
C5-6 level. The C8 root exits above the T1 pedicle at the C7-T1 level. Within the foramen,
the dorsal root is located more rostrally compared with the ventral root. The nerve roots
are in close proximity to the vertebral artery within the neuroforamen (Figure 2).
The borders of the cervical neuroforamen are the uncovertebral joint (ventromedial),
vertebral artery (lateral), inferior and superior articular processes of vertebra above and
below (dorsolateral), and suprajacent pedicle (superior).
Figure 2 Photograph of an axial cross-section of a spine shows the vertebral artery. Note
the proximity to the exiting nerve root (double arrowheads) and the uncovertebral joint
(UVJ). (Reproduced with permission from Williams KA, Rauschning W, Prasad S: Applied
anatomy of the cervical spine, in Steinmetz MP, Benzel EC, eds: Benzel's Spine Surgery E-
Book: Techniques, Complication Avoidance, and Management, ed 4. Philadelphia, PA,
Elsevier, 2016, pp 83-94.)

Etiology and Pathoanatomy
The clinical manifestations of cervical radiculopathy arise from a combination of nerve root
compression and inflammation.
Compressive lesions
Disk herniation
Soft disk herniation (Figure 3): nuclear material arising from an acute herniation may
impinge on the exiting nerve root posterolaterally, most commonly at its takeoff from the
spinal cord or laterally at the location where it traverses the neuroforamen.
Hard disk pathology (Figure 4): chronic disk degeneration with resultant disk height loss
may lead to a combination of annular bulging without frank herniation or the formation of
degenerative osteophytes that typically arise from the uncinate regions of the
posterolateral vertebral body (uncovertebral osteophytes).
Uncovertebral joint hypertrophy
Facet joint hypertrophy
Loss of disk height causing a decrease in the height of the intervertebral foramen and
buckling of the ligamentum flavum and/or the posterior longitudinal ligament
Inflammation
Compressive lesions, such as herniated disk material, may incite the production of
inflammatory cytokines, including interleukin-1 and interleukin-6, substance P, bradykinin,
tumor necrosis factor-α, and prostaglandins.

Etiology and Pathoanatomy
The clinical manifestations of cervical radiculopathy stem from a combination of
mechanical compression of the nerve root and the local inflammatory environment
related to that compression. Mechanical compression may be caused by any of the
structures surrounding the nerve roots and the nerve as they exit the neuroforamen.
Most common offending structures include a hard or soft disk herniation, uncovertebral
joint hypertrophy anteriorly, facet joint hypertrophy posteriorly, and loss of disk height
leading to buckling of the posterior longitudinal ligament and vertical stenosis within the
neuroforamen. The location of the compressive lesion should be noted because it may
guide surgical management.
In addition to mechanical deformation and focal vascular changes caused by nerve root
compression, various proinflammatory cytokines have been implicated in the
pathophysiology of cervical radiculopathy. Tumor necrosis factor-a has been
demonstrated to be released by local Schwann cells after nerve injury. The cytokine acts
synergistically with other proinflammatory cytokines, such as interleukin-1 and
interleukin-6. Release of tumor necrosis factor attracts macrophages to the site of injury,
resulting in additional upregulation of the proinflammatory response. In addition, tumor
necrosis factor induces local thrombus formation within the microvasculature supplying
the nerve root (Figure 5).

Natural History
Typically, acute cervical radiculopathy has a self-limiting course, with a rate of spontaneous
improvement as high as 75% (Resource 1).
A classic study by Lees and Turner assessed the natural history of cervical radiculopathy in 51
patients. Of these patients, 45% had resolution of pain after a single episode without
recurrence, 30% had mild continued symptoms, and 25% had persistent or worsening pain.

Natural History
In general, the natural history of cervical radiculopathy is variable, with a self-limiting
course in as many as 75% of patients. Therefore, nonsurgical symptomatic management
is the first line of treatment for patients with acute cervical radiculopathy. Large, natural
history studies are lacking on this topic. A classic study by Lees and Turner presented
long-term follow up (2 to 19 years) of 51 patients with cervical radiculopathy. The study
found that 45% of the patients had a self-limiting, single episode of pain without
recurrence; 30% of the patients had mild symptoms; and 25% of the patients had severe
or progressive symptoms. Nonsurgical treatment typically is the initial treatment option
for patients with cervical radiculopathy; however, randomized controlled trials that
demonstrate improvement of the favorable natural history of cervical radiculopathy via
specific nonsurgical treatment options are lacking.
Evaluation and Diagnosis
Patient History and Physical Examination
Patients frequently have unilateral neck pain that radiates ipsilaterally in a dermatomal
distribution of the affected root (Table 1).
 The most common levels of root involvement are C6 and C7.
 Less common levels of root involvement are C2, C3, and C4.
The absence of radiating symptoms in a dermatomal distribution does not rule out
symptomatic nerve root compression. In addition, as many as 80% of patients report
cervicogenic headaches.

Patients also may report upper trapezial and interscapular pain.
A physical examination should be performed to identify the nerve root involved; however,
crossover between myotomes and dermatomes may be present. Anomalous distribution of
myotomes and dermatomes is common.
Patients with a prefixed brachial plexus will have C4-C8 nerves comprising the brachial
plexus. Therefore, the nerve responsible for the deficit will be shifted cranially one level (eg,
C4 may innervate the normal C5 distribution).
Patients with a postfixed brachial plexus will have C6-T2 nerves comprising the brachial
plexus. Therefore, the nerve responsible for the deficit will be shifted caudally one level (eg,
C6 may innervate the normal C5 distribution).
Compressive lesions in the cervical spine tend to result in radiculopathy of the exiting nerve
root. For example, posterolateral C5-6 disk herniation and C5-6 foraminal stenosis from an
uncovertebral osteophyte usually results in C6 radiculopathy.
 Large central and paracentral disk herniations or stenosis may affect the subjacent root.

Patient History and Physical Examination
A thorough patient history and physical examination are critical in accurately identifying
cervical radiculopathy and ruling out other potential causes of neck and arm pain.
Factors that require delineation in the work up of patients in whom cervical
radiculopathy is suspected include pain location, radiation, duration of symptoms,
alleviating factors, and precipitating factors. Specifically, surgeons must identify if the
pain has a dermatomal distribution. Associated symptoms include decreased sensation
and weakness. Cervical radiculopathy should be suspected if the pain, decreased
sensation, and/or decreased motor function correspond with the same dermatomal
level or levels. Patients may have symptoms of myelopathy and radiculopathy; therefore,
surgeons must evaluate for issues with balance, fine motor skills, and bowel or bladder
control.
Physical examination includes inspection of the patient’s posture, general alignment, and
general muscle tone. Often, patients with long-standing weakness as a result of nerve
compression will have atrophy of involved musculature, especially in the hands. Range of
motion of the cervical spine is evaluated. A thorough motor examination is performed
for bilateral upper and lower extremities. Surgeons must examine the lower extremities
and the upper extremities to evaluate for possible tandem stenosis (combined cervical
and lumbar stenosis). Reflex testing and special maneuvers, including the Spurling test,
the Lhermitte sign, the Hoffman sign, ankle clonus, and the Babinski reflex, are then
performed.
Imaging Studies
Correlation between physical examination findings and MRI findings is pivotal in identifying the
etiology of cervical radiculopathy.

Imaging Studies
Imaging studies provide key clinical data on patients with signs and symptoms of cervical
radiculopathy. Plain radiographs are obtained as part of a standard evaluation and
include AP, lateral, and flexion and extension lateral views. Radiographs may
demonstrate signs of severe spondylosis, disk space narrowing, and overall alignment.
CT scans aid in evaluating bony architecture and are especially useful in identifying
patients with an ossified posterior longitudinal ligament. MRI is the main imaging
modality used to evaluate for cervical radiculopathy. MRI aids in identifying soft-tissue
lesions leading to compression of the cervical nerve roots (Figure 6).
Correlation between pathology identified on MRI and a patient’s clinical presentation
with regard to dermatomal distribution of symptoms and signs is a key step in creating a
treatment plan. Boden et al1 reported MRI evidence of degeneration in at least one
intervertebral disk in 57% of asymptomatic individuals older than 40 years. Daimon et
al2 performed a 20-year longitudinal study of 193 asymptomatic individuals. The study
revealed that, at baseline, MRI evidence of some degeneration was observed in more
than 20% of asymptomatic individuals younger than 70 years and in almost 80% of
asymptomatic individuals older than 70 years. Over the next 20 years, progression of
degenerative changes was observed on the MRIs of 95% of the individuals; however, no
relationship was reported between the progression of degenerative changes of the
intervertebral disk on MRI and the development of symptoms. Therefore, MRI findings
alone are insufficient in determining the presence of clinically important cervical
radiculopathy.

Differential Diagnosis
Differential diagnosis includes peripheral nerve entrapment syndromes (carpal or cubital
tunnel syndrome); brachial plexus injury; Parsonage-Turner syndrome; tendinopathies of the
shoulder, elbow, and wrist; and zoster neuritis.
Selective cervical nerve root injections may aid in confirming the source of symptoms if they
improve after injection.
Electromyography and nerve conduction velocity studies may help differentiate radiculopathy
from peripheral entrapment disorders; however, they should not be the sole determinant for

planning management because false-negative electrodiagnostic study results for radiculopathy
occur in as many as 50% of patients.
Differentiating cubital tunnel syndrome from C8-T1 radiculopathy (no test is perfect)
The ulnar nerve only innervates the ulnar two digits in the hand. The medial antebrachial
cutaneous (C8-T1) nerve innervates the ulnar forearm.
The ulnar nerve innervates all intrinsic muscles in the hand except the abductor pollicis
brevis, the flexor pollicis brevis, the opponens pollicis, and the lateral two lumbrical muscles
(median nerve via C8-T1). If all intrinsic muscles are weak, then the patient has median and
ulnar nerve compression or C8-T1 radiculopathy.
Visceral disorders (coronary artery disease and cholecystitis causing referred pain to the upper
extremity) also should be considered.

Differential Diagnosis
The most common presenting complaint of patients with cervical radiculopathy is upper
extremity pain or numbness with or without weakness. The differential diagnosis for this
patient presentation is fairly broad and includes peripheral nerve compression, cervical
myelopathy, thoracic outlet syndrome, Parsonage-Turner syndrome, and a Pancoast
tumor (Resource 2). Typically, patients with cervical radiculopathy have symptoms in a
dermatomal distribution that correlates with the location of pathologic findings on MRI.
Typically, patients with cervical radiculopathy report relief of symptoms as the upper
extremities are raised over the head (hand on head).
Carpal tunnel, cubital tunnel, and ulnar tunnel syndrome are three common peripheral
nerve compression syndromes that may result in symptoms similar to those of cervical
radiculopathy. Cubital tunnel and ulnar tunnel compression lead to symptoms of ulnar
nerve compression. This must be distinguished from C8 or T1 radiculopathy. Typically,
compression of the C8 root will lead to numbness of the entire ring finger and the little
finger, extending proximal to the wrist. Conversely, ulnar nerve compression leads to
numbness of one-half of the ring finger and the entire little finger, stopping at the wrist.
Sensation of the ulnar forearm proximal to the wrist is provided by the medial
antebrachial cutaneous nerve (C8-T1). In addition, the ulnar nerve innervates all intrinsic
muscles in the hand except the lateral two lumbricals, opponens pollicis, abductor

pollicis brevis, and flexor pollicis brevis, which are innervated by the median nerve (C8-
T1). If a patient has weakness of all the intrinsic muscles in the hand, then C8/T1
radiculopathy is more likely than isolated compression of the ulnar nerve.
Patients with carpal tunnel syndrome have decreased sensation in the thumb, the index
and long fingers, and one-half of the ring finger as a result of dysfunction of the median
nerve. This distribution is more consistent with C6 or C7 radiculopathy. Median nerve
compression at the carpal tunnel frequently results in dysfunction of the median nerve–
innervated intrinsic muscles listed previously. Patients with C6 and C7 radiculopathy
more commonly report weakness in elbow flexion and wrist extension (C6) or elbow
extension and wrist flexion (C7). Electromyography may help differentiate peripheral
nerve compression from cervical radiculopathy; however, electrodiagnostic study results
must be interpreted in the context of patient symptoms and signs.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
In general, the natural history of cervical radiculopathy is favorable.
Nonsurgical management is the initial treatment option; however, controlled trials comparing
various nonsurgical treatment options (such as physical therapy, modalities, traction,
medications, manipulation, and immobilization) with no treatment are lacking.
Techniques/Procedures
Cervical collar
Immobilization in a cervical collar is thought to diminish inflammation about an irritated
nerve root and may relieve muscle spasm.
The efficacy of cervical collars in limiting the duration or severity of radiculopathy has not
been demonstrated.
Prolonged immobilization (>1 to 2 weeks) should be avoided.
Traction
The benefits of home traction have not been proven.
Traction should be avoided in patients with myelopathy.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:38 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000050
15/24

Medications
NSAIDs: no proven long-term benefit with regard to altering the natural history of cervical
radiculopathy; may be beneficial for short-term symptom management.
Patients being treated via long-term NSAID therapy should be monitored for kidney and
gastrointestinal toxicity and hepatotoxicity (more common with long-term acetaminophen
therapy).
Selective cyclooxygenase-2 inhibitors reduce the incidence of adverse gastrointestinal
effects; however, in controlled trials of patients with osteoarthritis, cyclooxygenase-2
inhibitors did not appear to be more efficacious than nonselective NSAIDs.
Opioid analgesic agents
Although opioids may result in short-term relief of severe pain, their substantial adverse-
effect profile and addictive potential make them a poor treatment option for the
management of cervical radiculopathy.
Antidepressants and gabapentin are used in the management of chronic neuropathic pain
syndromes.
Oral corticosteroids
Anecdotally, these drugs are effective in diminishing acute radicular pain; however, oral
corticosteroids have not been reported to favorably alter the long-term natural history of
cervical radiculopathy.
Rare but substantial complications, such as infection, hyperglycemia, and osteonecrosis, may
occur.
Physical therapy
Physical therapy may be beneficial but has not been reported to alter the natural history of
cervical radiculopathy.
Massage and modalities, such as heat, ice, electrical stimulation, and ultrasonography, have
not been proven to be beneficial.
Postural education, ergonomics, and lifestyle modifications may be beneficial.
Isometric exercises to strengthen the cervical musculature are instituted as acute pain
resolves.
Aerobic conditioning may help relieve symptoms.
Cervical adjustment (chiropractic manipulation)
The efficacy of cervical manipulation has not been established.
For neck pain and cervicogenic headaches, cervical manipulation affords short-term benefits,
with a complication rate of 0.5 to 1.0 per 1 million manipulations.
Cervical steroid injections

These injections commonly are used in the nonsurgical management of radiculopathy
(lumbar and cervical).
Injections allow for specific targeting of the problematic root(s) and the dorsal root
ganglion, resulting in a greater local concentration of steroid at the desired location.
They provide diagnostic information by blocking the pain associated with a symptomatic
root. This is especially useful in localizing the level causing pain because anomalous
distributions are common.
Although some observational studies report long-lasting relief in 50% to 70% of patients who
undergo epidural steroid injections for the management of cervical radiculopathy, this is
comparable to the natural history of the disease.

Nonsurgical Management
Nonsurgical management is the initial treatment option for patients with cervical
radiculopathy. Because approximately 75% of patients with cervical radiculopathy will
experience a resolution of symptoms or continued mild symptoms without any
treatment, the focus of nonsurgical management is the short-term control of symptoms.
High-quality randomized controlled trials that demonstrate improvement of the natural
history of cervical radiculopathy via nonsurgical management are lacking.
Typically, patients are offered physical therapy and NSAIDs for the initial management of
cervical radiculopathy. Although neither of these nonsurgical treatment modalities has
been proven to alter the natural history of cervical radiculopathy, they may aid in short-
term symptom control as the condition improves as part of its natural course. A history
of preexisting medical conditions should be elicited to determine if contraindications to
NSAID consumption, such as peptic ulcer disease, gastritis, or kidney issues, exist.
Cervical chiropractic manipulation does not offer any lasting benefits and may pose a
risk to patients, with a documented complication rate of 0.5 to 1 per 1 million
manipulations. Opioid analgesic agents should be avoided in patients with cervical
radiculopathy because of their addictive potential and the substantial adverse-effect
profile. Cervical epidural steroid injections may be of diagnostic benefit; however, the
effectiveness of such injections has not been documented in placebo-controlled

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000050
17/24

randomized trials. Interlaminar injections have the potential to spread across multiple
levels, which limits the evaluation of a single level from a diagnostic perspective but may
aid in evaluation of the contribution of the cervical spine to overall pain/symptoms.
Surgical Management
Indications for surgical management include severe or progressive neurologic deficit
(weakness or numbness) or substantial pain that fails to respond to nonsurgical management.
Techniques/Procedures
Anterior cervical diskectomy and fusion (ACDF)
Advantages
ACDF allows for the direct removal of most lesions causing cervical radiculopathy
(herniated disks, uncovertebral spurs) without neural retraction (Figure 7).
Placement of an anterior bone graft in the disk space opens the neuroforamen in the
craniocaudal direction, thereby providing indirect decompression of the nerve root.
Associated fusion may improve axial neck pain arising from disk degeneration and
spondylosis; however, this is less predictable than relief of neurogenic pain.
Anterior incisions tend to be aesthetically preferable but are associated with risks of
recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy and dysphagia, particularly during multilevel surgery.
ACDF requires minimal muscle dissection and generally is associated with little
perioperative pain and rapid recovery.
Disadvantages
Fusion may lead to increased mechanical stress on adjacent levels. Current evidence,
although inconclusive, suggests that this mechanical stress may lead to an increased rate of
adjacent segment degeneration.
ACDF may result in pseudarthrosis and graft-related complications.
Factors affecting the rate of pseudarthrosis include patient variables (smoking, age,
autoimmune disease), graft type (autograft versus allograft), the attempted number of
fusion levels, and plating.
Currently, ACDF with an allograft and a plate is a popular treatment option for cervical
radiculopathy at one or two levels to avoid donor-site morbidity and because the use of
allograft results in acceptable outcomes.

Studies show equivalent fusion rates between ACDF with an autograft and ACDF with an
allograft and a plate.
Persistent speech and swallowing complications (2% to 5%) are associated with anterior
exposure and retraction of the esophagus and the laryngeal nerve.
Superior laryngeal nerve palsy
Rare complication that results in increased aspiration risk from impaired gag reflex and in
impairment of high-pitch singing.

cervical diskectomy and fusion with the use of autograft shows a well-incorporated fusion; the
clinical result was excellent. (Reproduced from Albert TJ, Murrell SE: Surgical management of
cervical radiculopathy. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 1999;7[6]:368-376.)
Cervical disk replacement (CDR)
CDR is a well-studied motion-preserving treatment option for a select group of patients with
cervical radiculopathy.

Several randomized controlled trials sponsored by the FDA have been completed, with
continued follow-up to 7 years demonstrating noninferiority of CDR compared with ACDF.
Traditional indications studied in investigational device exemption trials included patients
with one- or two-level disease and radicular symptoms recalcitrant to 6 weeks of nonsurgical
management.
Importantly, most studies excluded patients older than 65 years who had facet pathology
observed on imaging studies; signs of instability, such as more than 11° of angular
difference to adjacent levels or more than 3.5 mm of translation; cervical trauma;
substantial myelopathy; or previous cervical spine surgery.
Subsequent studies have evaluated expanded indications for CDR, such as replacement
adjacent to a site of prior fusion or in patients with myelopathy, but are of lower quality
compared with initial investigational device exemption trials, which adhered to strict
randomized controlled trial protocol.
The surgical approach and the method of neural decompression are essentially identical to
that used in ACDF. An artificial disk rather than a graft is placed in the decompressed disk
space.
Advantages
The major advantage of CDR is motion preservation. In theory, this should avoid the
increased mechanical stress placed on segments adjacent to the site of fusion.
Current research suggests that carefully selected patients who undergo CDR have a
lower rate of radiographic adjacent segment degeneration and clinically important
adjacent segment disease leading to revision surgery.
This data is from randomized controlled trials that included strict traditional CDR
indications.
An additional advantage of CDR is that, unlike ACDF, CDR does not depend on fusion for
effectiveness.
Disadvantages
Limited surgical indications compared with ACDF
Mechanical complications related to implant malpositioning
Technically demanding procedure requiring precise mechanical alignment of the implant
in the disk space for optimal results/longevity
Heterotopic ossification is a complication unique to CDR and has been reported in
approximately 16% to 60% of managed levels; however, the rate of heterotopic
ossification has been reported to decrease with use of NSAIDs postoperatively. The
clinical importance of heterotopic ossification remains unknown (Resource 3).

Posterior Cervical Foraminotomy
Posterior cervical foraminotomy can be performed to decompress the nerve root without
substantially destabilizing the spine in patients with lateral disk herniations leading to
foraminal stenosis.
The compressive disk herniation must be far enough lateral for a posterior foraminotomy to
afford adequate access.
Advantages
Avoids fusion
Reported success rate as high as 91.5%
Higher rate of return to play in professional athletes, with shorter time to return to play
Disadvantages
Possibility for incomplete decompression in patients with anterior compression lesions
Higher revision surgery rate compared with ACDF
Inability to restore disk and foraminal height at the diseased level
Potential for continued deterioration of the involved level

Surgical Management
Surgical treatment is reserved for patients with persistent symptoms of cervical
radiculopathy in whom nonsurgical treatment fails. The three most common surgical
treatment options for the management of cervical radiculopathy are ACDF, CDR, and
posterior cervical foraminotomy.
ACDF has a long history of success, with reported improvement in symptoms in 80% to
90% of patients. Originally, ACDF involved the use of iliac crest autograft as the graft
material of choice; however, the morbidity associated with iliac crest harvest can be
avoided. The use of an allograft in combination with a plate results in fusion rates similar
to those associated with the use of a structural iliac crest autograft. Other graft options
include titanium and polyether ether ketone cages. No single graft is superior to
another. An anterior approach is well tolerated by patients, leaves a cosmetically
favorable scar, and is well suited for the management of various pathologies. A
disadvantage of fusing a segment of the cervical spine is increased mechanical stress on
adjacent segments. Numerous biomechanical studies suggest that this increased

mechanical stress may lead to increased rates of radiographic adjacent segment
degeneration and clinical adjacent segment disease.
CDR was designed to preserve motion at the surgical level, thereby decreasing
mechanical stress on adjacent levels and decreasing the rate of adjacent segment
disease. The causative association between mechanical stress and adjacent segment
disease has not been proven. Numerous randomized controlled trials have assessed
CDR in a narrowly defined sample of patients with cervical radiculopathy at one or two
levels without substantial degeneration of the facet joints or evidence of instability. The
results of these studies, which recently reported 7- and 9-year follow-up data, are
promising. CDR and ACDF resulted in comparable rates of symptomatic improvement,
with lower rates of secondary procedures and radiographic adjacent segment
degeneration reported in the CDR cohorts. In a meta-analysis of 29 randomized
controlled trials, Dong et al reported that CDR was associated with lower rates of
radiographic adjacent segment degeneration and secondary surgery at adjacent levels
compared with ACDF (Resource 3). CDR is a good treatment option for select patients
who match the criteria identified in initial randomized controlled trials.
Posterior cervical foraminotomy is another motion preserving treatment option for the
management of cervical radiculopathy. This treatment option is best suited for the
management pathology that is far enough lateral so that it can be accessed with minimal
retraction of the nerve root via a posterior approach. Classically, this is a lateral soft disk
herniation. Posterior cervical foraminotomy is associated with a lower rate of morbidity
and faster recovery compared with ACDF. A study reported that a higher proportion of
professional athletes returned to sports activity after posterior cervical foraminotomy,
with a shorter time to return to sports activity, compared with ACDF. However, posterior
cervical foraminotomy is associated with a higher rate of revision surgery compared with
ACDF.
